items.q: Brand safety is about keeping ads away from content that could harm a brand.
items.why: Advertisers do not want their ads next to content that conflicts with their values.

items.q: Invalid traffic includes bots and other visits that are not real viewing.
items.why: Buyers should not pay for impressions no real person could see.

items.q: One tool can remove ad fraud completely.
items.why: Fraud keeps changing, so protection needs several layers and regular checks.

items.q: Verification vendors can check where an ad ran and whether it was viewable.
items.why: Independent checks give buyers confidence in what they paid for.

items.q: Malvertising is an ad that tries to deliver something harmful.
items.why: Examples include ads that redirect people or try to install unwanted software.

items.q: Brand suitability is exactly the same as brand safety for every brand.
items.why: Safety is a common minimum. Suitability depends on what is right for each brand.

items.q: A blocklist is a list of sites or categories where ads must not appear.
items.why: An allowlist is the opposite: the only places ads may appear.

items.q: Pre-bid blocking stops a bad impression before a bid, while post-bid reports show it after the ad ran.
items.why: Pre-bid prevents the spend. Post-bid helps you learn and block next time.

items.q: Domain spoofing is when a low-quality site pretends to be a more valuable one.
items.why: Buyers pay premium prices for what is really cheap inventory.

items.q: Ads that slow a page down can count as poor ad quality.
items.why: Heavy ads hurt the visitor’s experience even if they are not fraudulent.
